question: Walk through the proposed intended use, the patient, product-quality and data decisions it will support, and the evidence used to draw the GxP system boundary before funding was approved.
Show how the concept team identified the predicate records, signatures, retention duties and inspection-access obligations for every jurisdiction and regulated business process in scope.

Describe the proposed data lifecycle from first capture through processing, review, reporting, retention and destruction, and show where the concept explicitly protects attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, complete, consistent, enduring and available data.

Demonstrate how the concept distinguishes source data, raw data, metadata, official records, convenience copies and hybrid components, and how the authoritative version will be identified during an inspection.
Explain how preliminary risk assessment differentiated patient-safety, product-quality and data-integrity harm, and how that analysis changed scope, controls, budget or schedule.
Show how the business case funds documented evidence that the system will remain fit for intended use across configuration, testing, release, operation, change and retirement.
Walk through the proposed shared-responsibility model and show which GxP controls remain with the regulated company when infrastructure, administration, backup or release activity is outsourced.
Demonstrate that the concept and procurement timetable allow risk-based supplier evaluation, technical assessment, audit where warranted, and remediation before supplier lock-in.

Describe the proposed identity lifecycle and authorization model from onboarding through role change, periodic review, emergency access and termination, and show how it supports attribution and least privilege.

Explain the proposed separation between business processing, record review, security administration, configuration and audit-trail oversight, including how a small operating team will control unavoidable conflicts.
Show how the concept determines which actions require electronic signatures, their meaning, identity proofing, credential controls and permanent linkage to the signed record.

Walk through every proposed inbound and outbound interface, identifying the authoritative source, transformation, timing, error owner, reconciliation point and retained evidence for each critical data element.
Demonstrate how the business case accounts for migrating or preserving legacy records, metadata, audit trails, signatures and relationships while maintaining value and meaning.
Define each proposed algorithmic use, the decisions it may influence, the authoritative inputs and outputs, and the point at which a qualified human remains accountable for a GxP decision.

Explain how the concept identifies auditable events, preserves who/what/when/why, prevents audit-trail disablement, and resources risk-based review within the business process rather than as a technical afterthought.

Show how the concept identifies infrastructure and platform services that must be qualified or controlled to support the validated application, including clocks, databases, identity, networks and monitoring.
Demonstrate how required retention periods, readable retrieval, metadata/audit-trail preservation, legal holds and inspector access were converted into lifecycle cost and architecture assumptions.

Explain how proposed recovery objectives were derived from product, patient, data and operational impact, and show that exact and complete backup plus restoration verification are included in cost and responsibilities.

Walk through the proposed business-continuity process during prolonged system or interface loss, including controlled manual records, approvals, inventory/status control and reconciliation after service restoration.

Show how the operating model will assess supplier releases, configuration and infrastructure changes, perform proportionate regression, approve deployment and periodically confirm the system remains fit for intended use.

Describe how technical alerts, user errors, data-integrity concerns, security events and supplier incidents will enter the pharmaceutical quality system for impact assessment, investigation, CAPA and timely escalation.

Demonstrate that the business case identifies the competencies and capacity needed for process ownership, configuration, validation, data review, administration, supplier oversight and support throughout the lifecycle.
Present the major compliance assumptions and trade-offs in the approved business case and show how changes to cost, schedule or scope trigger independent quality reassessment and go/no-go decisions.

Explain how proposed benefits and performance indicators avoid incentivizing delayed recording, data exclusion, unofficial testing, inappropriate reprocessing or closure of exceptions without adequate investigation.

Show how the concept funds an exit strategy that preserves readable GxP records, metadata, audit trails, signatures, configurations and retrieval capability after contract termination or technology obsolescence.

Explain how business, quality, technical and data owners converted the approved intended use into the URS, and show how conflicts, assumptions, exclusions and unresolved requirements are governed before design begins.

Trace each intended use and predicate-record obligation into specific URS requirements for creation, review, approval, retention, retrieval and inspection, including functions outside the primary application boundary.

Show how critical process steps, data elements, metadata, calculations, reports and configurations are identified in the URS and linked to preliminary risk decisions without using priority labels as a substitute for compliance.

Demonstrate how each URS statement expresses an observable outcome, boundary condition and acceptance criterion that can establish fitness for intended use rather than merely repeating policy words such as secure, compliant or user-friendly.

Describe the URS requirements that preserve the full record context—originator, event time, system time, units, status, method, version, reason and relationships—from first capture through every transformation.

Walk through the URS audit-event matrix and show how requirements capture secure, computer-generated, time-stamped who/what/when/why history for record, configuration, security and critical master-data changes without obscuring the prior value.

Show how the URS turns audit-trail review into a usable control by specifying reviewer views, context, filters, exception logic, review timing, evidence of completion and escalation before the associated quality decision.
Demonstrate how the URS specifies unique attribution, role-based least privilege, joiner/mover/leaver timing, periodic review and ownership for human, service, interface and robotic identities.

Explain how requirements separate record creation, approval, configuration, security administration, audit review and release, and how unavoidable conflicts and emergency access are independently authorized, logged and reviewed.

Trace each regulated approval into URS requirements for signer identity, date/time, signature meaning, authentication, non-repudiation and permanent linkage to the exact record version and human-readable copy.

Walk through each critical workflow and show how the URS requires permitted sequence, prerequisite evidence, role authority, status transitions and prevention or controlled override of out-of-order processing.

Explain how the URS differentiates input sources and requires validity, completeness, range, format, unit, identifier and duplicate checks while preserving rejected attempts and controlled corrections where they are GxP-relevant.

Show how each interface requirement defines source and target records, field-level transformations, units/precision, identifiers, sequencing, acknowledgements, retries, duplicate control, reconciliation and retention of transmission evidence.
Demonstrate how the URS defines each GxP calculation or rule, authoritative inputs, version, units, precision, rounding, boundary behavior, invalid/missing-data handling and reproducible output.

Explain how the URS identifies critical configuration and master data, assigns creation/change/approval authority, preserves effective versions and prevents unapproved values from influencing records.

Show how requirements identify the complete original electronic record and specify accurate, complete, human-readable and electronic copies that preserve needed metadata, audit history, relationships and dynamic review capability.

Describe how the URS requires preservation or justified archival of legacy values, metadata, audit trails, signatures, status, links and record meaning, including reconciliation and handling of invalid or unmappable data.

Trace every record category to a requirement for retention start event, period, archive format, metadata/audit history, readability test, legal hold, authorized destruction and documented evidence of disposition.
Show how the URS specifies exact and complete backup scope, frequency, protection, separation, monitoring and periodic restoration with reconciliation to justified RPO and RTO.
Walk through URS requirements for controlled offline operation during application, interface, identity or site outages and for complete, duplicate-free reconciliation when service returns.

Explain how the URS converts the GxP threat model into requirements for authentication, encryption, secure configuration, vulnerability handling, event logging, clock synchronization, monitoring and protection of data at rest and in transit.

Demonstrate how customer requirements define supplier versus company responsibilities for validation evidence, configuration, access, backup, incidents, changes, subcontractors, data location, inspection support and exit.

Show how the URS specifies control and evidence for configuration/code changes, supplier releases, emergency changes, incident detection, affected-record analysis, CAPA and periodic evaluation of validated state.
Explain how user and administrator requirements address workload, clear status, error prevention, accessibility, reviewer context, training environment and demonstrable competence for critical tasks.

Define URS requirements for every AI-enabled function covering intended use, prohibited decisions, data provenance, model/version identity, performance limits, explainability, qualified human review, drift monitoring, change and fallback.

Walk through the risk-assessment method, decision rules and governance used for this system, and demonstrate how the level of formality and documentation is proportionate to uncertainty, complexity and potential harm.

Demonstrate how the risk boundary follows the complete intended use across application, infrastructure, interfaces, records, people, procedures and external services rather than the procurement boundary.

Explain the categorisation rationale for each software and infrastructure component and show how category, novelty, configurability and actual intended use influence—but do not replace—function-level risk and assurance decisions.

Show how the assessment decomposed the system into software modules, configurations, custom code, reports, interfaces, infrastructure and supplier services at a level where distinct failure modes and controls can be evaluated.
For each critical function, explain the credible failure modes and causal path from incorrect, missing, delayed or unauthorized system behavior to patient safety, product quality or supply impact.
Demonstrate how the assessment combines data criticality with lifecycle vulnerability and detectability for raw data, metadata, audit trails, derived results, master data and reports.

Show how the assessment distinguishes predicate-rule risk, Part 11 electronic-record controls and electronic-signature controls, and how each applicable clause maps to functions and risks without treating compliance as a negotiable score.

Explain how the risk assessment evaluates impersonation, orphaned access, excessive privilege, conflicting duties, direct database access, service accounts and supplier administration across the identity lifecycle.
Demonstrate how risk determines auditable events, protection, reason capture, review timing and reviewer context for data, configuration, access and administrative actions.

Walk through failure scenarios for identity proofing, credential sharing, signature meaning, authentication, record-version linkage, timestamp and post-signature change, and show how risk controls each scenario.
For every interface, show how the assessment addresses partial, duplicate, delayed, out-of-order, corrupted, unmapped and unauthorized transfers plus transformation, precision and time-zone errors.
Explain how migration risks cover selection, extraction, transformation, mapping, load, reconciliation and preservation of metadata, audit trails, signatures, links and record meaning.

Demonstrate how supplier criticality is derived from reliance, product complexity, evidence transparency, regulated experience, quality-system maturity, support model and ability to remediate defects.

Map each GxP control to provider, subprocessor and regulated-company responsibilities, then show how tenancy, location, concentration, privileged support, evidence access and service termination affect risk.

Show how cybersecurity threats are translated into GxP harm scenarios involving unauthorized change, loss of chronology, unavailable records, corrupted backups, altered configuration or compromised interfaces.
For each critical calculation or rule, demonstrate analysis of wrong formula/version, precision, rounding, unit, boundary, missing input, stale reference data and nonreproducible result.

Explain how the assessment evaluates data provenance, model limitations, bias, nondeterminism, drift, prompt/input manipulation, silent provider change, explainability and automation bias for each GxP use.
Show how risks from operating systems, databases, networks, time services, identity, virtualization, orchestration and monitoring are assessed in relation to application controls and validated state.

Derive maximum tolerable outage, RTO and RPO from GxP process impact and analyze failure of application, interface, identity, site and supplier, including risks introduced by manual fallback and reconciliation.

Distinguish archive and backup risks and show how the assessment covers retention duration, readability, metadata/audit-history completeness, legal holds, obsolescence, corruption, restore and authorized destruction.
Demonstrate how each function/data risk determines the type, rigor, independence and retained evidence of assurance activities while all applicable requirements remain verified.
Show how the assessment considers task complexity, interface design, workload, fatigue, ambiguous roles, training effectiveness, staff turnover and dependence on manual detective controls.

Explain how defects, deviations, security events, audit findings, recalls, workarounds and prior changes from this product, supplier and predecessor system informed failure likelihood and control selection.

For every high or critical inherent risk, demonstrate that selected controls are specific, implemented by a named owner, testable, sustainable in operation and sufficient to justify the residual-risk conclusion.

Define the events and evidence that will trigger risk reassessment—requirements/design changes, supplier releases, incidents, drift, new threats, performance trends, periodic evaluation and retirement—and show how prior assumptions remain traceable.

Explain how supplier criticality was determined from intended use, control reliance, data access, service substitutability, complexity and failure impact, and show how that rating set the depth of due diligence and approval.

Walk through the supplier QMS from leadership oversight through document control, training, deviation/CAPA, change, internal audit and management review, and demonstrate its effectiveness with recent records rather than policy statements.
Demonstrate how the supplier controls requirements, architecture, secure coding, code review, configuration, testing, release, maintenance and retirement for the exact product and version proposed.

Show how regulated-domain competence, inspection/customer history, defect trends, organizational stability, financial viability and product roadmap were evaluated against the required service life and retention horizon.

Walk through the deployed architecture and identify standard functions, tenant configuration, custom code, low-code components, reports, integrations and shared services, showing which lifecycle evidence and owner covers each.

Demonstrate how supplier specifications, testing, certifications and release evidence are evaluated for relevance to the customer's exact version, configuration, intended use and risk before being leveraged.

Trace how test data, expected results, execution identity/time, environment, actual outcomes, deviations and defects are controlled so that passing status cannot be created by excluding failed or repeated runs.

Explain how the supplier's security governance, risk management, independent assessments and certifications apply to the exact service, regions and subprocessors, and how gaps are translated into GxP risk rather than accepted by badge.

Demonstrate how supplier employees, contractors, service accounts and emergency users are identity-proofed, authorized, segregated, monitored, periodically reviewed and revoked for customer environments.

Show how the product automatically captures and protects who, what, when and why for relevant record, configuration, master-data, access and administrator events, including prior/new values and customer control over enablement.

Walk through the shared-responsibility model and demonstrate how tenant isolation, configuration boundaries, monitoring, backup, encryption, changes and evidence delivery operate for the proposed service architecture.
Identify every subprocessor that can host, access, change, transmit, back up or support GxP data/services, and demonstrate risk-based qualification, contractual flow-down and ongoing change control.
Map where primary data, metadata, audit trails, backups, support copies and telemetry reside and who owns or controls each throughout active service, suspension, dispute and termination.

Demonstrate how the supplier specifies, tests and controls interface schemas, transformations, authentication, acknowledgements, retries, idempotency, error handling, version compatibility and retained transmission evidence.
Show the exact backup scope, schedules, retention, isolation, encryption, monitoring and restoration process for tenant data, metadata, audit trails, configuration, files and keys.

Demonstrate how the supplier derived and tested availability, capacity, RTO and RPO across application and external dependencies, and how customers are informed and supported during regional or prolonged disruption.

Demonstrate that the service can retain and retrieve complete readable records—including metadata, audit trails, attachments, signatures and relationships—for customer-defined periods and provide accurate human-readable and electronic copies promptly.

Show how the supplier implements signer identity, date/time, meaning, reauthentication and inseparable linkage to the exact record version across user interface, API, export, archive and disaster recovery.

Trace the supplier's change process from request and impact assessment through design, test, approval, deployment, rollback and customer notification, including emergency changes and tenant configuration.

Demonstrate how the supplier identifies GxP-relevant service, data-integrity and security incidents, preserves evidence, determines affected tenants/records, performs root cause and CAPA, and notifies customers in time for product decisions.
Walk through vulnerability intake, GxP/security impact assessment, prioritization, patch testing, deployment, exception, monitoring and end-of-support planning for all product dependencies.

Demonstrate how remote support is requested, authorized, time-limited, supervised, recorded and reviewed, including direct database/file access, data extracts, diagnostic copies and actions performed outside application controls.

Show how the supplier defines, verifies and maintains competence for developers, testers, quality reviewers, administrators, incident responders and support personnel whose work affects customer GxP controls.

Demonstrate the supplier's control of AI intended use, training/reference data provenance, model development, evaluation, versioning, prompts/configuration, monitoring, human oversight, security and customer notification of behavioral change.

Reconcile the qualification findings with the executed contract and quality agreement, showing enforceable ownership, evidence delivery, change/incident notice, audit/regulator access, retention, CAPA, subprocessor and exit obligations.

Demonstrate how every approved URS requirement and risk control is allocated to functional, configuration, technical and procedural design, with bidirectional traceability through unresolved decisions and approved exclusions.

Walk through the logical and physical design from user and instrument to identity, application, middleware, databases, monitoring, backup and archive, showing how every GxP dependency is controlled and qualified where applicable.

Explain how the design model represents raw/source data, metadata, event and entry times, units, status, method/configuration versions, relationships, provenance and invalidated values throughout the data lifecycle.

Demonstrate at field and event level how the design creates secure computer-generated time-stamped history showing who, what, when and why, including prior/new values, failed or prohibited actions where relevant, and changes by privileged or automated actors.

Show how the design converts raw audit events into contextual, risk-based reviewer views with source-record drill-down, filters, exception logic, review period, reviewer identity, completion evidence and escalation before disposition or release.

Walk through the permission model from business role to object, action, data scope and workflow state, showing unique attribution, least privilege, inheritance, conflicting rights and default-deny behavior.

Demonstrate how the design separates administration from GxP processing and approval, limits direct data access, controls emergency privilege and provides independent, tamper-resistant oversight of every privileged action.

Explain how identity proofing, unique identifiers, MFA, credential issuance/reset, lockout, session timeout, reauthentication and nonhuman secrets are designed across normal, offline, recovery and support modes.

Trace the signature transaction from record rendering and signer reauthentication through stored identity, date/time, meaning, record-version digest/linkage, manifestation, export and archival retrieval.

Use the state model to demonstrate permitted transitions, prerequisites, role authority, status visibility, concurrency control, override conditions and audit behavior for normal and exceptional GxP workflows.

Show how each input channel validates source, identity, format, unit, range, sequence, completeness and duplication while distinguishing original event time from later entry and preserving controlled corrections or invalidations.

For every critical formula and rule, identify authoritative inputs, source reference, version, units, precision, rounding, boundary/missing-data behavior, effective date and stored evidence needed to reproduce the result.

Walk each critical field and metadata element through the interface design, including schema/version, source authority, transformation, precision, authentication, sequencing, acknowledgement, retry, idempotency, error queue and reconciliation.

Demonstrate how critical configuration, specifications, limits, methods, templates and reference data are created, verified, approved, activated, versioned, linked to records, changed, rolled back and retired.

Show how each report and export is derived from authoritative data and preserves required context, filters, units, versions, metadata, signatures and audit history so the output is accurate, complete and readily inspectable.

Explain how the migration design preserves value and meaning for data, metadata, audit trails, signatures, attachments, links and statuses, and how repeatable extraction, transformation, reconciliation, exception handling and rollback work.

Trace the complete record set across transactional storage, files, indexes, audit stores, configuration, encryption keys and backups, showing integrity protection, failure detection, RPO and validated restoration/reconciliation.

Demonstrate how record-class retention start events, linked-object dependencies, archive format/viewer, readability checks, legal holds, authorized purge and destruction evidence are implemented without severing context.

Walk through design behavior during application, interface, identity, network and supplier outages, including controlled offline records, unique identifiers, event times, authority, queued transactions and complete reconciliation after recovery.

Show how the design protects GxP confidentiality, integrity, chronology and availability through trust boundaries, encryption/key management, secure configuration, trusted time, security monitoring and preserved forensic evidence.

Demonstrate how specifications, code, configuration, master data, infrastructure and supplier releases are versioned, promoted through segregated environments, impact-assessed, tested, approved, deployed and rolled back while preserving the production baseline.

Show how monitoring, application errors, audit events, interface queues, security alerts and user reports feed a design that preserves evidence, identifies affected records/batches, supports root cause and links incidents to deviations, CAPA and change.

Reconcile the technical design with the quality agreement and shared-responsibility matrix for tenant configuration, privileged access, audit evidence, change, backup, incidents, data location, subprocessors, inspection and exit.

Explain the design for model and prompt/version control, input/output provenance, performance boundaries, nondeterminism, human review, drift, security, adverse-output handling, supplier updates, reproducibility and fallback for each GxP use.

Demonstrate that the specifications expose observable outcomes, diagnostic evidence and controllable test conditions for critical normal, boundary, negative, recovery and misuse cases, and that design outputs define role-specific training and competence needs.

Walk me through how every GxP-relevant configuration item in the implemented build is derived from an approved requirement or design decision and how unauthorized or undocumented settings are detected before testing.

Demonstrate how the regulated user established that internal and supplier development activities operated under an appropriate quality system, including defect control, review independence, records retention, and release discipline.

Show how traceability proves both that every approved GxP requirement is implemented and tested and that every GxP-relevant code or configuration element has a justified upstream requirement and risk control.
Explain how source code, scripts, configuration-as-code, and report definitions are protected so that the approved version can be attributed, reviewed, reproduced, and linked to the deployed release.

Walk me through the controlled promotion path from development to test to production and show how the process prevents developers or suppliers from introducing untested content directly into the production-bound package.

Demonstrate how development, administration, testing, release approval, and production deployment privileges are separated according to risk and how unavoidable conflicts are detected and independently reviewed.
Show how review depth and reviewer independence are determined from GxP risk and how the review establishes more than stylistic compliance for critical logic and configuration.

Demonstrate how the organization establishes provenance for each production-bound artifact, including source revision, dependency versions, build environment, compiler or interpreter, build identity, and integrity verification.

Explain how third-party libraries, containers, plugins, and embedded components are inventoried, approved, monitored for vulnerability and obsolescence, and assessed for GxP impact before inclusion in a release.

Show how insecure defaults, sample accounts, diagnostic functions, unnecessary services, and excessive permissions are identified and removed or justified in the configured solution before qualification.

Demonstrate how the audit-trail design identifies all GxP-relevant create, modify, delete, approve, invalidate, configuration, security, and administrative events and preserves the prior value, actor, time, object, and reason where required.

Show how the configured electronic-signature function preserves signer identity, date and time, signature meaning, record linkage, credential control, and prevention of signature reuse across every regulated signing context.

Explain how critical inputs are validated at every entry path and how invalid, incomplete, out-of-sequence, duplicate, or malicious inputs are rejected or quarantined without loss of the original attempt and context.

Demonstrate how each regulated interface proves completeness, correct sequence, uniqueness, authenticity, and reconciliation from source creation through final processing, including retries and partial failures.
Show how GxP calculations, rounding, unit conversion, limits, status logic, and decision rules are specified, independently reviewed, and verified against authoritative reference results.
Explain how database schemas, stored procedures, triggers, views, retention jobs, and direct data-fix scripts are versioned, reviewed, tested, and reconciled to the approved application release.

Demonstrate how credentials, API tokens, encryption keys, and certificates used by the configured system are generated, stored, rotated, recovered, revoked, and prevented from entering source code, test evidence, or logs.

Show how the design preserves trustworthy event chronology across clients, servers, databases, interfaces, cloud services, and devices when time zones, daylight-saving changes, offline operation, or clock drift occur.

Explain how the configured solution makes processing failures visible, preserves diagnostic and business context, prevents silent continuation, and supports controlled recovery without altering original regulated records.

Demonstrate how the build identifies every component and datum required for a consistent recovery, including application, database, files, configuration, audit trails, keys, interfaces, and scheduler state.

Show how migration or conversion tooling preserves the value, context, metadata, relationships, audit history, signatures, and meaning of regulated records and produces independently verifiable reconciliation evidence.

Demonstrate how automated test tools, frameworks, scripts, simulators, and test environments were assessed as adequate for their intended use and how false passes, stale scripts, and unverified test data are prevented.

Explain how test data are designed to exercise GxP failure modes while preventing unauthorized use of live personal, patient, product, or confidential production records and preserving test reproducibility.

Show how cloud infrastructure, platform services, network policy, identity, logging, storage, backup, and region settings are defined as controlled configuration and reconciled to the qualified deployed state.

Demonstrate how low-code workflows, rules, forms, reports, dashboards, templates, and other administrator-configurable objects are treated as controlled software when they influence GxP records or decisions.

Walk me through how the IQ protocol scope was derived from the approved architecture, system description, risk assessment, supplier documentation, and prerequisite qualification status rather than from a generic installation template.

Demonstrate how the as-installed inventory identifies each GxP-relevant hardware, virtual resource, operating system, database, middleware, application, agent, library, interface component, and managed service with version and ownership.

Show how the installed physical and logical architecture, data flows, interfaces, prerequisites, and security boundaries were verified against the approved design and how every variance was dispositioned.

Explain how each installed environment is uniquely identified and segregated so that users, integrations, credentials, jobs, data, and deployment paths cannot be confused across development, test, qualification, training, and production.
Demonstrate how operating-system, database, middleware, runtime, and platform installations were verified against approved versions, options, patches, locale, services, and support prerequisites.
Show how the virtual-machine, hypervisor, cluster, container image, orchestration, and persistent-storage foundation supporting the application was qualified and tied to the application IQ boundary.
Demonstrate how installed network routes, ports, protocols, firewall rules, proxies, remote-access paths, and trust boundaries were verified against the minimum approved connectivity design.

Show how authentication integration with the identity provider was installed and verified, including tenant or domain, protocol, claims, groups, fail-safe behavior, certificate trust, and prevention of unintended local-account fallback.

Demonstrate how every installed service, integration, database, scheduler, and automation account is uniquely inventoried, owned, least-privileged, non-interactive where appropriate, and linked to a controlled secret.
Show how authoritative time synchronization, timezone, daylight-saving behavior, and drift monitoring were installed and verified across every system layer that creates or orders regulated events.

Demonstrate how installed certificates, trust stores, encryption settings, and keys match the approved security design and remain recoverable, monitorable, and attributable throughout their lifecycle.

Show how database and storage installations were verified for location, capacity, redundancy, integrity protection, access, encryption, transaction/log settings, retention, and separation of regulated records from transient data.

Demonstrate how every required application, database, file, configuration, audit-trail, key, and scheduler component was enrolled in backup with the approved frequency, retention, protection, and monitoring.

Show how health monitoring, application and security logging, alerting, endpoint protection, integrity monitoring, and log forwarding were installed on every in-scope component and verified as active.

Demonstrate that required audit trails and administrative logs were enabled before regulated configuration or data creation and that their storage, access, time source, and retention settings match the approved design.
Show how identity, authentication, time, certificate, and record-linking dependencies required for electronic signatures were installed and verified before functional signature testing.
Demonstrate that every approved interface endpoint, queue, topic, connector, schema, route, certificate, service account, and error store was installed in the correct environment and version.

Show how the regulated user verified the correct cloud tenant, account, subscription, region, availability model, managed services, data locations, logging, backup features, and shared responsibilities for the qualified instance.

Demonstrate how the qualified SaaS version, feature set, tenant configuration, enabled modules, extensions, and provider release channel were identified at IQ and protected from unnoticed change before OQ.

Show how connected instruments, controllers, terminals, scanners, printers, sensors, or other devices were uniquely identified, correctly installed, calibrated or qualified where required, and mapped to the computerized system.

Demonstrate how current supplier operating instructions, maintenance requirements, compatibility information, installation records, and licenses were collected, reviewed for suitability, controlled, and handed to accountable owners.
Show how supplier installation scripts, checklists, certificates, and executed records were reviewed and independently confirmed by the regulated user before being accepted as IQ evidence.

Demonstrate that the installed hardening baseline is effective across application, operating system, database, middleware, cloud, and device layers and that every privileged access path is known and controlled.

Explain how IQ deviations, unexpected results, missing prerequisites, and as-built discrepancies were investigated for root cause and cumulative impact rather than closed individually as documentation issues.

Demonstrate how responsible personnel concluded that the installed system and infrastructure were suitable to enter OQ, including treatment of open items, baseline lock, document approval, and confirmation that the object to be tested is unchanged.

Show how the OQ strategy converts documented GxP and data-integrity risks into test coverage for functions, limits, error handling, security, records, interfaces, and recovery without allowing low-risk labels to hide critical control interactions.

Demonstrate how tester competence, independence, environment access, and data preparation were controlled so OQ results provide an objective challenge rather than confirmation by the people who configured the function.

Walk me through how OQ proves that each critical functional control operates as specified, remains traceable to an approved requirement, and cannot be bypassed through alternate screens, APIs, imports, jobs, or administrator functions.

Show how upper and lower operating limits and credible worst-case combinations were derived from process knowledge and challenged in OQ, including behavior just inside and outside each accepted boundary.

Demonstrate how OQ challenges invalid data, missing prerequisites, unavailable dependencies, interrupted transactions, unauthorized sequence, and partial failure while proving no silent loss, corruption, or uncontrolled continuation.
Show how OQ proves complete and accurate audit-trail capture for risk-relevant creation, modification, deletion, approval, invalidation, configuration, security, and administrative events.

Demonstrate that authorized reviewers can retrieve, filter, sequence, interpret, annotate, and retain complete audit-trail evidence for a defined review period without relying on privileged database support.
Show how OQ challenges the permitted and prohibited actions of each GxP role, including cross-role conflicts, privileged functions, inherited access, and direct data or configuration paths.
Demonstrate how provisioning, modification, suspension, transfer, termination, recertification, and emergency-access workflows operate across all integrated identity and application layers.
Show how OQ challenges authentication, failed attempts, lockout, timeout, re-authentication, concurrent sessions, token revocation, password or MFA controls, and emergency access according to risk.

Demonstrate through adverse testing that electronic signatures remain unique, authenticated, meaning-specific, time-stamped, permanently linked, and non-transferable when records are copied, changed, exported, restored, or viewed later.

Show how OQ proves that human-readable and electronic copies are accurate, complete, intelligible, and suitable for inspection, including metadata, audit history, signatures, units, attachments, and context.

Demonstrate how OQ challenges the full lifecycle of critical data so records remain attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original or true copy, accurate, complete, consistent, enduring, and available.
Show how OQ verifies the configured additional accuracy check for critical manually entered data, including independence, source comparison, correction, override, and audit behavior.
Demonstrate under normal and adverse conditions that each critical interface preserves completeness, value, meaning, sequence, uniqueness, security, and end-to-end reconciliation.
Show how OQ independently verifies critical reports, dashboards, calculations, filters, totals, rounding, units, time periods, exports, and drill-down against authoritative source data.

Demonstrate through OQ that backup and restore functions recover a consistent, readable, accurate, and complete system state, including configuration, audit trails, signatures, attachments, keys, and interface state.

Show how OQ challenges component failure and failover while proving transaction consistency, controlled user experience, alerting, recovery timing, and return to normal service without untraceable manual intervention.

Demonstrate how OQ verifies scheduled and background jobs for correct sequence, dependencies, calendars, retries, duplicate prevention, late or missed execution, output reconciliation, and operator intervention.

Show how OQ proves that alerts detect loss of service, processing failure, data-integrity exceptions, capacity threats, security events, backup failures, and interface backlog with actionable context and accountable routing.
Demonstrate that OQ challenges anticipated peak load, data volume, concurrency, latency, storage growth, and long-running operations while preserving control effectiveness and record accuracy.
Show how OQ challenges time zones, daylight-saving transitions, clock drift, leap dates, offline events, and out-of-order messages while preserving unambiguous chronology and business-rule timing.

Demonstrate through OQ that migration and conversion routines preserve value and meaning across supported record types, metadata, relationships, signatures, audit histories, attachments, units, and character sets.

Explain how OQ failures are preserved, investigated, corrected, impact-assessed, regression-tested, and independently reviewed without replacing the original evidence or narrowing acceptance criteria after seeing results.

Demonstrate how the OQ report establishes that the configured system operates as designed throughout its anticipated range and is suitable for PQ/UAT, including open defects, deviations, residual risks, baseline identity, and procedural readiness.
Walk me through how PQ/UAT demonstrates that the complete configured system supports its approved intended use within the real GxP business process, not merely that individual functions passed OQ.

Demonstrate that the PQ/UAT environment is sufficiently equivalent to the production environment for the tested process, data volume, interfaces, security, devices, timing, and operational controls, and justify every material difference.

Show how business and quality owners defined acceptance, selected representative scenarios, reviewed actual evidence, and accepted residual risk rather than delegating PQ/UAT judgment entirely to IT or the supplier.
